rows.subtopic: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds
rows.stem: The oxidation number of Pt in \(\mathrm{[Pt(en)_2Cl_2]^{2+}}\) is :
rows.solution:
The complex ion as a whole carries \(+2\). Inside it, the two ethane-1,2-diamine ligands are neutral and the two chlorido ligands contribute \(-1\) each, so they together contribute \(-2\). For the ion to come out at \(+2\), platinum must supply \(+4\):
\(x + 2(0) + 2(-1) = +2 \implies x = +4\)
The oxidation number of platinum is \(+4\). Reading the \(+2\) of the ion straight off as the metal's oxidation state is the trap, and it ignores the two negative ligands inside the sphere.

rows.stem: Which of the following product is formed when salicylic acid is treated with \(\mathrm{(CH_3CO)_2O}\) in the presence of acid ?

options.label: A
options.text: a benzene ring bearing \(\mathrm{-COOCH_3}\) and \(\mathrm{-OH}\) on adjacent carbon atoms

options.label: B
options.text: a benzene ring bearing \(\mathrm{-OCOCH_3}\) and \(\mathrm{-OH}\) on adjacent carbon atoms

options.label: C
options.text: a benzene ring bearing \(\mathrm{-COCH_3}\) and \(\mathrm{-COOH}\) on adjacent carbon atoms

options.label: D
options.text: a benzene ring bearing \(\mathrm{-OCOCH_3}\) and \(\mathrm{-COOH}\) on adjacent carbon atoms

rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — all four options are DRAWN structures and the stem names none of them. Read at 2.5x zoom: every ring shows explicit alternating double bonds (genuine benzene, unlike the PLAIN hexagons in this same paper's Q28(b)) and every one is ORTHO-disubstituted. Rendered by SUBSTITUENT PATTERN rather than by compound name deliberately — naming (D) as aspirin/acetylsalicylic acid would state the answer, whereas the substituent reading is lossless and preserves the discrimination the question tests. Page idx 4.
rows.solution:
Salicylic acid is 2-hydroxybenzoic acid, and acetic anhydride acetylates its phenolic \(-\mathrm{OH}\) group, leaving the carboxyl group untouched. The product is acetylsalicylic acid, better known as aspirin — a benzene ring carrying \(-\mathrm{OCOCH_3}\) and \(-\mathrm{COOH}\) on adjacent carbons.

Two of the distractors invert the connectivity: \(-\mathrm{COOCH_3}\) would be an ester of the CARBOXYL group, formed with methanol rather than with acetic anhydride, and \(-\mathrm{COCH_3}\) would be a ketone, the product of a Friedel-Crafts acylation on the ring. The oxygen must stay between the ring and the acetyl group.

rows.stem: Which reagent is used to distinguish between primary, secondary and tertiary amines ?
rows.solution:
Hinsberg's reagent, benzenesulphonyl chloride, separates all three classes in a single test. With a PRIMARY amine the sulphonamide formed still carries a hydrogen on nitrogen; that hydrogen is acidic, so the product dissolves in alkali. With a SECONDARY amine the nitrogen has no hydrogen left after the reaction, so the sulphonamide is insoluble in alkali. A TERTIARY amine has no hydrogen on nitrogen to substitute and does not react at all.

Benzoyl chloride reacts with primary and secondary amines but does not distinguish them as cleanly; the carbylamine test responds only to primary amines; and the iodoform test has nothing to do with amines.

rows.stem: The correct order of decreasing basic strength in aqueous solution of the following is :
rows.solution:
In water three effects act together and do not point the same way. The ethyl groups release electron density onto nitrogen and raise basicity. Steric crowding lowers it, since bulky groups obstruct the approaching proton. And solvation lowers it too: the more hydrogens a cation has on nitrogen, the more hydrogen bonds it can make to water, so the primary amine's cation is best stabilised and the tertiary amine's worst.

For ethyl groups these settle out with the secondary amine strongest, the tertiary next and the primary last:
\((\mathrm{C_2H_5})_2\mathrm{NH} > (\mathrm{C_2H_5})_3\mathrm{N} > \mathrm{C_2H_5NH_2}\)
This order must be remembered as it stands, because for METHYL groups the answer differs — there the primary amine outranks the tertiary.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem: Which of the following transition metals shows \(+1\) and \(+2\) oxidation states ?
rows.solution:
Copper shows both \(+1\) and \(+2\). Its configuration is \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^{10} 4s^1\), so losing the single \(4s\) electron gives \(\mathrm{Cu^{+}}\), \(3d^{10}\), and losing one more from the d subshell gives \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\), \(3d^9\). Both are common — cuprous and cupric compounds alike.

Scandium shows only \(+3\), zinc only \(+2\), and manganese runs from \(+2\) to \(+7\) but does not show \(+1\) in ordinary compounds.

rows.stem: On hydrolysis, which of the following carbohydrates gives only \(\beta\)-glucose ?
rows.solution: Cellulose is a straight-chain polysaccharide built entirely from \(\beta\)-D-glucose units joined by \(\beta\)-1,4 glycosidic linkages, so hydrolysis gives \(\beta\)-glucose and nothing else. Starch and maltose are built from \(\alpha\)-D-glucose, so they give the \(\alpha\) anomer, and sucrose gives glucose together with fructose. The \(\alpha\)-versus-\(\beta\) difference is exactly why humans digest starch and cannot digest cellulose: our enzymes hydrolyse the \(\alpha\) linkage only.

rows.stem:
Consider the following compounds :
Chlorobenzene (I), 2,4,6-trinitrochlorobenzene (II), 2,4-dinitrochlorobenzene (III), 4-nitrochlorobenzene (IV)
The correct order of increasing ease of nucleophilic substitution reactions of these compounds is :
rows.solution:
Nucleophilic substitution on an aryl halide is made easier by electron-WITHDRAWING groups at the ortho and para positions, because they stabilise by resonance the negative charge of the intermediate formed when the nucleophile attacks. The more such groups, the easier the reaction.

Chlorobenzene has none and is the least reactive. 4-Nitrochlorobenzene has one, 2,4-dinitrochlorobenzene has two, and 2,4,6-trinitrochlorobenzene has three. The increasing order of ease is therefore
chlorobenzene \(<\) 4-nitrochlorobenzene \(<\) 2,4-dinitrochlorobenzene \(<\) 2,4,6-trinitrochlorobenzene, that is I \(<\) IV \(<\) III \(<\) II.

Note that a nitro group at the META position would not help, since the intermediate's charge cannot reach it.

rows.stem:
The half-life periods of decomposition of \(\mathrm{NH_3}\) for different initial pressures are given below :

| p (torr) | 704 | 75 | \(34{\cdot}5\) |
|---|---|---|---|
| \(\mathrm{t_{1/2}}\) (min) | 80 | 80 | 80 |

The order of the reaction is :
rows.solution:
The half-life is 80 minutes at every initial pressure — 704 torr, 75 torr and 34.5 torr alike. Independence of the starting amount is the signature of FIRST order, where
\(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{k}\)
contains no concentration term at all.

For any other order the half-life would move with the initial pressure: for zero order \(t_{1/2} \propto [\mathrm{R}]_0\), so it would fall twentyfold across this range, and for second order \(t_{1/2} \propto 1/[\mathrm{R}]_0\), so it would rise. The data are therefore enough to fix the order without any calculation.

rows.stem: 1 mole of liquid A and 2 moles of liquid B make a solution having a total vapour pressure 40 torr. The vapour pressure of pure A and pure B are 30 torr and 45 torr respectively. The above solution :

options.label: B
options.text: shows negative deviation from Raoult’s Law.

options.label: C
options.text: shows positive deviation from Raoult’s Law.

rows.solution:
Test the mixture against what Raoult's law predicts. The mole fractions are \(x_A = \tfrac{1}{3}\) and \(x_B = \tfrac{2}{3}\), so the predicted total vapour pressure is
\(p = x_A p_A^{\circ} + x_B p_B^{\circ} = \tfrac{1}{3}(30) + \tfrac{2}{3}(45) = 10 + 30 = 40\ \mathrm{torr}\)

The observed total pressure is also 40 torr. Prediction and observation agree exactly, so there is no deviation in either direction and the solution is ideal.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Ethers have lower boiling points than the boiling points of alcohols.
Reason (R) : This is due to the presence of hydrogen bonding in alcohols.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Ethers do boil lower than alcohols of comparable molecular mass, so the Assertion is true, and alcohols do have hydrogen bonding, so the Reason is true.

The marking scheme judges the Reason not to be the full explanation, and the reason for that judgement is that the comparison has two halves. Alcohols hydrogen bond to one another because they have a hydrogen attached to oxygen; ethers have NO hydrogen on oxygen at all, so their molecules cannot hydrogen bond to each other and are held together only by weaker dipole-dipole and van der Waals forces. The Reason states the first half and leaves out the second. Both statements are true, but the Reason is treated as an incomplete account rather than the explanation of the Assertion.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Transition metals show their highest oxidation state with oxygen.
Reason (R) : The ability of oxygen to form multiple bonds to metals.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution: Transition metals do reach their highest oxidation states in combination with oxygen — manganese gets to \(+7\) only in \(\mathrm{MnO_4^-}\) and \(\mathrm{Mn_2O_7}\), chromium to \(+6\) only in its oxo species — so the Assertion is true. Oxygen's ability to form multiple bonds to the metal is real, and it is the cause: a small, highly electronegative atom that can donate electron density back through \(\pi\) bonding stabilises the metal in a very high oxidation state in a way a singly bonded ligand cannot. Fluorine is the other ligand that reaches such states, by being small and electronegative rather than by multiple bonding. The Reason is therefore the correct explanation of the Assertion.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Monobromination of aniline can be conveniently done by protecting the amino group by acetylation.
Reason (R) : Acetylation increases the activation effect of the amino group.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Monobromination of aniline really is done by acetylating first, so the Assertion is true. Without protection the \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\) group activates the ring so strongly that bromine water gives 2,4,6-tribromoaniline at once, and stopping at one substitution is impossible.

The Reason inverts the point of the protection. Acetylation converts \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\) into \(-\mathrm{NHCOCH_3}\), whose nitrogen lone pair is partly drawn away by the carbonyl group, so the ring is LESS strongly activated, not more. It is that reduction in activating power which makes monosubstitution possible. So the Assertion is true while the Reason is false.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Order of reaction is applicable to elementary as well as complex reactions.
Reason (R) : For a complex reaction, molecularity has no meaning.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Order applies to elementary and complex reactions alike, because it is read off the experimentally determined rate law and every reaction has one. So the Assertion is true. Molecularity has no meaning for a complex reaction, because it counts the species colliding in a SINGLE elementary step and a multi-step reaction has no single step to count. So the Reason is true as well.

But the Reason is a statement about molecularity, not about order. That molecularity fails for complex reactions does not explain why ORDER succeeds for them. Both are true but the Reason is not the explanation of the Assertion — the two statements are the complementary halves of one contrast rather than cause and effect.

rows.stem:
How do you explain the following ?
(a) Presence of an aldehyde group in glucose
(b) Presence of a primary alcoholic group in glucose
rows.solution:
(a) The aldehyde group. Bromine water is a MILD oxidising agent: it attacks an aldehyde group and leaves alcohols alone. With glucose it gives the six-carbon monocarboxylic acid, gluconic acid:
\(\mathrm{CHO(CHOH)_4CH_2OH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Br_2\ water}} \mathrm{COOH(CHOH)_4CH_2OH}\)
Only an aldehyde would be oxidised under these conditions, so the carbonyl in glucose must be an aldehyde and not a ketone. Its reduction of Tollens' reagent says the same thing.

(b) The primary alcoholic group. Concentrated nitric acid is the stronger oxidant and gives the DICARBOXYLIC saccharic acid:
\(\mathrm{CHO(CHOH)_4CH_2OH} \xrightarrow{\text{conc. }\mathrm{HNO_3}} \mathrm{COOH(CHOH)_4COOH}\)
The second carboxyl group has to have come from somewhere, and it comes from the other end of the chain. Only a PRIMARY alcohol, \(-\mathrm{CH_2OH}\), can be oxidised to \(-\mathrm{COOH}\); a secondary one would stop at a ketone. So the carbon at the far end of the chain carries a primary alcoholic group.

rows.stem:
How will you obtain the following from aniline ? Write the chemical equations involved :
(a) Sulphanilic acid
(b) 2,4,6-Tribromoaniline
(c) Acetanilide
rows.solution:
(a) Sulphanilic acid. Aniline is treated with concentrated sulphuric acid, which first protonates the nitrogen to give anilinium hydrogensulphate; heating that to \(453-473\ \mathrm{K}\) rearranges it, and the sulphonic acid group ends up para to the amino group.
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_2SO_4}} \mathrm{C_6H_5\overset{+}{N}H_3\,HSO_4^-} \xrightarrow{453-473\ \mathrm{K}} \mathrm{4\text{-}H_2N{-}C_6H_4{-}SO_3H}\)
The product exists largely as its zwitterion, which is why it melts so high and dissolves so poorly.

(b) 2,4,6-Tribromoaniline. Bromine water needs no catalyst: the \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\) group activates the ring so strongly that all three available positions are brominated at once, and the product separates as a white precipitate.
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2} + 3\mathrm{Br_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Br_2}/\mathrm{H_2O}} \mathrm{2,4,6\text{-}Br_3{-}C_6H_2{-}NH_2} + 3\mathrm{HBr}\)
Stopping at one bromine is precisely what cannot be done without first acetylating the nitrogen.

(c) Acetanilide. Acetic anhydride, usually in pyridine, acetylates the nitrogen; the pyridine removes the acetic acid formed and drives the reaction forward.
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2} + (\mathrm{CH_3CO})_2\mathrm{O} \xrightarrow{\text{pyridine}} \mathrm{C_6H_5NHCOCH_3} + \mathrm{CH_3COOH}\)

rows.stem:
Give reasons for the following :
(a) Haloalkanes react with KCN to form alkyl cyanides, while with AgCN, they form isocyanides.
(b) \(\mathrm{C_6H_{11}-CH_2-Cl}\) (a cyclohexane ring bearing \(\mathrm{-CH_2-Cl}\)) is more reactive towards \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) displacement as compared to \(\mathrm{C_6H_{11}-Cl}\) (a cyclohexane ring bearing \(\mathrm{-Cl}\)).
(c) Grignard reagents should be prepared under anhydrous conditions.
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE — sub-part (b) names neither compound in words; both are DRAWN as rings. Read at 3x zoom: both are PLAIN hexagons with NO inner circle and NO alternating double bonds, i.e. CYCLOHEXANE, not benzene — and the contrast is decisive inside this one paper, because Q3's option structures on idx 4 DO show explicit alternating double bonds. Corroborated independently by this paper's own marking scheme (ms idx 5), which explains the difference as 'C ... is 1° whereas ... is 2°' — a primary/secondary distinction that only makes sense for cyclohexylmethyl chloride vs cyclohexyl chloride, and would be wrong for benzyl chloride vs chlorobenzene. Named losslessly in the stem, so the row is answerable from text. Page idx 12.
rows.solution:
(a) The cyanide ion is AMBIDENT — it can attack through carbon or through nitrogen — and which end attacks depends on how the reagent holds it. Potassium cyanide is predominantly ionic, so in solution it releases a free cyanide ion, whose carbon is the stronger nucleophile; attack through carbon gives the alkyl cyanide, \(\mathrm{R-CN}\). Silver cyanide is largely covalent, so the carbon is tied up in the bond to silver and only the nitrogen lone pair is available; attack through nitrogen gives the isocyanide, \(\mathrm{R-NC}\).

(b) An \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) reaction requires the nucleophile to approach the carbon from the side opposite the leaving group, so the less crowded that carbon is, the faster the reaction. In \(\mathrm{C_6H_{11}-CH_2-Cl}\) the chlorine sits on a PRIMARY carbon, which carries two hydrogens and only one bulky group; in \(\mathrm{C_6H_{11}-Cl}\) it sits on a SECONDARY carbon of the ring, flanked on both sides by ring carbons that block the approach. The primary halide is therefore the more reactive.

(c) A Grignard reagent, \(\mathrm{R-MgX}\), has a strongly polarised carbon-magnesium bond in which the carbon carries a substantial negative charge, so it behaves as a powerful base as well as a nucleophile. Even a trace of water protonates it at once, destroying the reagent and giving the alkane:
\(\mathrm{R-MgX} + \mathrm{H_2O} \longrightarrow \mathrm{R-H} + \mathrm{Mg(OH)X}\)
The reagent must therefore be prepared and used in dry ether under anhydrous conditions, and for the same reason it cannot be used on any substrate carrying an \(-\mathrm{OH}\), \(-\mathrm{NH_2}\) or \(-\mathrm{COOH}\) group.
